extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students/practitioners of humor, rhetoric, and public speaking; Mark Twain readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit evaluative criteria for writing and delivering humorous public speeches: preparation, performance, audience adaptation, comic techniques (surprise, irony, hyperbole), pacing, and confidence. Grounded in Mark Twain's own speeches and commentary on oratory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance doubles the author's words
rubrics_metrics.description: “He always held that the actor doubled the value of the author's words; and he was a great actor as well as a great author.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain/Howells assert that delivery/performance amplifies the written text's effect — effective speech depends not only on the words but on acting, voice, and presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative as well as representative acting
rubrics_metrics.description: “Representation is the art of other actors; his art was creative as well as representative; it was nothing at second hand.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't merely imitate or 'represent' text; invent original fancies and thoughts that the voice and action will realize — bring new, personally-created material to performance rather than merely reproducing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough preparation and memorization
rubrics_metrics.description: “He studied every word and syllable, and memorized them by a system of mnemonics peculiar to himself ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully craft and learn your text; preparation includes word-level study so the delivery is controlled and precise rather than improvised or unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mnemonic systems to fix structure
rubrics_metrics.description: “...a system of mnemonics peculiar to himself, consisting of an arbitrary arrangement of things on a table—knives, forks, salt-cellars; inkstands, pens, boxes, or whatever was at hand—which stood for points and clauses and climaxes...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize the speech with physical or mental anchors for points and climaxes so memory and pacing are reliable; mnemonic devices can help manage complex structure in performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study tone, gesture, and forecast audience reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: “He studied every tone and every gesture, and he forecast the result with the real audience from its result with that imagined audience.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice not only words but vocal tones and physical gestures; rehearse with an imagined audience to predict reactions and shape emphasis and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when to stop (brevity and restraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: “he rejoiced in the pleasure he gave and the blows of surprise which he dealt; and because he had his end in mind, he knew when to stop.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a clear sense of the speech's endpoint; avoid overextending jokes or anecdotes — effective humor often depends on well-timed restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence in delivery — don't show fear
rubrics_metrics.description: “you can't be successfully funny if you show that you are afraid of it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commit fully to the comic material; visible hesitation, doubt, or fear undermines the audience's willingness to take the joke as intended and can kill laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and manage audience sensibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Twain's account of a failed Boston performance: the audience's 'black frost' and 'petrified' faces suggest a mismatch between material and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of cultural, regional, or institutional sensitivities of your audience; material that is acceptable or hilarious in one context can be disastrous in another. Tailor tone and targets accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use surprise and comic 'blows' for effect
rubrics_metrics.description: “he rejoiced in the pleasure he gave and the blows of surprise which he dealt;”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ surprise, unexpected twists, and sudden shifts of tone as active devices in humor — well-placed surprises produce strong comic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft matter that is 'glad, honest, kind, just'
rubrics_metrics.description: Howells: “The matter the reader has here before him; and it is good matter, glad, honest, kind, just.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality material for speeches/humor should have ethical/sympathetic qualities — being glad, honest, kind, and just increases audience goodwill and the lasting value of the comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in consumption of 'nonsense' (audience guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: “If I sell to the reader this volume of nonsense, and he, instead of seasoning his graver reading with a chapter of it now and then, unwisely overdoses himself with several chapters of it at a single sitting, he will deserve to be nauseated...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reader/audience guidance: humorous material is most effective when consumed in balance with more serious reading — overconsumption may blunt appreciation or create fatigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical techniques: irony, contrast, hyperbole, mock-formality
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout speeches (e.g., 'Plymouth Rock and the Pilgrims') Twain uses satire, rhetorical questions, ironic praise, and hyperbole to lampoon ancestral pride.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective comic rhetoric uses well-chosen devices — irony, exaggerated contrast, mock solemnity, rhetorical questioning — to expose absurdities and produce laughter while making a point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of program context and sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Twain's failed speech harmed subsequent speakers (Bishop's inability to 'make good') — showing how one performance can affect the program's momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider your place in an event's sequence; an ill-judged or ill-received piece can derail the flow for others. Adjust content/length/tone to support the occasion's overall programme.
